The rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes is xy=kxy = kxy=k.

#Introduction: the Cartesian plane

Analytic geometry translates geometry into algebra: a point becomes a pair of numbers, a line or a curve becomes an equation in xxx and yyy. In this way geometric problems are solved with equations, systems and inequalities, and conversely an equation can be “seen” as a figure.

#The Cartesian coordinate system

Definition 5.1 Cartesian coordinate system

A Cartesian coordinate system is formed by two perpendicular oriented lines that meet at the origin OOO: the axis of abscissas (xxx-axis, horizontal, oriented to the right) and the axis of ordinates (yyy-axis, vertical, oriented upwards). The real numbers are represented on both of them, with 000 at OOO. Every point PPP corresponds to exactly one ordered pair P=(x,y)P = (x, y)P=(x,y): xxx is the xxx-coordinate (abscissa) of PPP, yyy is its yyy-coordinate (ordinate).

The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise starting from the positive xxx-axis. Points lying on the axes do not belong to any quadrant: on the xxx-axis they have y=0y = 0y=0, on the yyy-axis they have x=0x = 0x=0.

QuadrantSigns of the coordinatesExample
Ix>0x > 0x>0, y>0y > 0y>0P=(3,2)P = (3, 2)P=(3,2)
IIx<0x < 0x<0, y>0y > 0y>0Q=(−2,3)Q = (-2, 3)Q=(−2,3)
IIIx<0x < 0x<0, y<0y < 0y<0R=(−3,−2)R = (-3, -2)R=(−3,−2)
IVx>0x > 0x>0, y<0y < 0y<0S=(2,−3)S = (2, -3)S=(2,−3)
Note Symmetric points

You will need them with conics and with functions. The point symmetric to P=(x,y)P = (x, y)P=(x,y) with respect to the xxx-axis is (x,−y)(x, -y)(x,−y); with respect to the yyy-axis it is (−x,y)(-x, y)(−x,y); with respect to the origin it is (−x,−y)(-x, -y)(−x,−y); with respect to the bisector y=xy = xy=x it is (y,x)(y, x)(y,x), that is, the coordinates are swapped.

Example 5.1 A point and its symmetric points

P=(−1,4)P = (-1, 4)P=(−1,4) has a negative xxx-coordinate and a positive yyy-coordinate: it lies in quadrant II. Its symmetric point with respect to the xxx-axis is (−1,−4)(-1, -4)(−1,−4), in quadrant III; with respect to the yyy-axis it is (1,4)(1, 4)(1,4), in quadrant I; with respect to the origin it is (1,−4)(1, -4)(1,−4), in quadrant IV; with respect to the bisector y=xy = xy=x it is (4,−1)(4, -1)(4,−1), in quadrant IV.

#Distance between two points

Rule 5.1 Distance between two points

The distance between A=(xA,yA)A = (x_A, y_A)A=(xA​,yA​) and B=(xB,yB)B = (x_B, y_B)B=(xB​,yB​) is

d(A,B)=(xB−xA)2+(yB−yA)2d(A, B) = \sqrt{(x_B - x_A)^2 + (y_B - y_A)^2}d(A,B)=(xB​−xA​)2+(yB​−yA​)2​

You do not need to learn it by heart: it is Pythagoras' theorem. The segment ABABAB is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with a horizontal leg of length ∣xB−xA∣|x_B - x_A|∣xB​−xA​∣ and a vertical leg of length ∣yB−yA∣|y_B - y_A|∣yB​−yA​∣ (the bars ∣…∣|\ldots|∣…∣ denote the absolute value). The differences are squared, so the order of the subtraction does not matter. If the two points have the same yyy-coordinate, the distance is simply ∣xB−xA∣|x_B - x_A|∣xB​−xA​∣; if they have the same xxx-coordinate, it is ∣yB−yA∣|y_B - y_A|∣yB​−yA​∣.

Example 5.2 Two distances

A=(1,2)A = (1, 2)A=(1,2), B=(4,6)B = (4, 6)B=(4,6): d=(4−1)2+(6−2)2=9+16=25=5d = \sqrt{(4 - 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5d=(4−1)2+(6−2)2​=9+16​=25​=5.

A=(−2,−1)A = (-2, -1)A=(−2,−1), B=(4,1)B = (4, 1)B=(4,1): xB−xA=4−(−2)=6x_B - x_A = 4 - (-2) = 6xB​−xA​=4−(−2)=6 and yB−yA=1−(−1)=2y_B - y_A = 1 - (-1) = 2yB​−yA​=1−(−1)=2, so d=36+4=40=210d = \sqrt{36 + 4} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}d=36+4​=40​=210​.

Common mistake The minus signs

With negative coordinates it is easy to get the subtraction wrong: 4−(−2)=64 - (-2) = 64−(−2)=6, not 222. Always write the brackets before substituting.

#Midpoint of a segment

Rule 5.2 Midpoint

The coordinates of the midpoint of the segment ABABAB are the averages of the coordinates of the endpoints:

M=(xA+xB2,yA+yB2)M = \left(\frac{x_A + x_B}{2}, \frac{y_A + y_B}{2}\right)M=(2xA​+xB​​,2yA​+yB​​)
Example 5.3 Midpoint and the inverse problem

A=(−3,5)A = (-3, 5)A=(−3,5), B=(7,−1)B = (7, -1)B=(7,−1): M=(−3+72,5−12)=(2,2)M = \left(\frac{-3 + 7}{2}, \frac{5 - 1}{2}\right) = (2, 2)M=(2−3+7​,25−1​)=(2,2).

Inverse problem: M=(3,1)M = (3, 1)M=(3,1) is the midpoint of ABABAB and A=(1,−2)A = (1, -2)A=(1,−2); find BBB. From 1+xB2=3\frac{1 + x_B}{2} = 321+xB​​=3 you get xB=5x_B = 5xB​=5; from −2+yB2=1\frac{-2 + y_B}{2} = 12−2+yB​​=1 you get yB=4y_B = 4yB​=4. So B=(5,4)B = (5, 4)B=(5,4), which is also the point symmetric to AAA with respect to MMM.

In the test Distances without a calculator

Pythagorean triples save time: if the differences of the coordinates are 333 and 444 (or 666 and 888, 555 and 121212, 888 and 151515), the distance is 555 (or 101010, 131313, 171717) without computing any roots. If the result is a root, simplify it: 40=4⋅10=210\sqrt{40} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 10} = 2\sqrt{10}40​=4⋅10​=210​. To find a point “equidistant” from two given points, set the squares of the distances equal: the roots disappear and the second-degree terms cancel out.

#5.1 The straight line in the Cartesian plane

In this unit every line is described by a first-degree equation in xxx and yyy. A point belongs to a line (or to any curve) if and only if its coordinates, substituted into the equation, make it true.

#Special lines

  • The xxx-axis is made up of the points with yyy-coordinate zero: its equation is y=0y = 0y=0. The yyy-axis has equation x=0x = 0x=0.
  • Horizontal lines, parallel to the xxx-axis, have equation y=ky = ky=k: all their points have yyy-coordinate kkk. Vertical lines, parallel to the yyy-axis, have equation x=hx = hx=h.
  • The lines through the origin, except the yyy-axis, have equation y=mxy = mxy=mx: for each of their points (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) with x≠0x \ne 0x=0 the ratio yx\frac{y}{x}xy​ is always mmm.
  • The bisector (bisettrice) of quadrants I and III contains the points with equal coordinates, of the form (x,x)(x, x)(x,x): its equation is y=xy = xy=x. The bisector of quadrants II and IV contains the points (x,−x)(x, -x)(x,−x): its equation is y=−xy = -xy=−x.
Example 5.4 Lines through a point parallel to the axes

The vertical line through (5,−2)(5, -2)(5,−2) is x=5x = 5x=5 (all its points have xxx-coordinate 555); the horizontal line through the same point is y=−2y = -2y=−2. The point (−3,3)(-3, 3)(−3,3) lies on the bisector y=−xy = -xy=−x, because 3=−(−3)3 = -(-3)3=−(−3); it does not lie on the bisector y=xy = xy=x.

#Slope-intercept form: slope and y-intercept

Definition 5.2 Slope-intercept form

A non-vertical line has equation y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q. The number mmm is the slope (or gradient; in Italian coefficiente angolare or pendenza), the number qqq is the yyy-intercept (ordinata all'origine): the line crosses the yyy-axis at the point (0,q)(0, q)(0,q).

The slope measures how steeply the line rises: if xxx increases by 111, yyy increases by mmm. Taking any two points AAA and BBB on the line,

m=ΔyΔx=yB−yAxB−xAm = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{y_B - y_A}{x_B - x_A}m=ΔxΔy​=xB​−xA​yB​−yA​​

where Δ\DeltaΔ (read “delta”) denotes a change: Δx\Delta xΔx is how much the xxx-coordinate changes, Δy\Delta yΔy how much the yyy-coordinate changes. It is also true that m=tan⁡αm = \tan\alpham=tanα, where α\alphaα (read “alpha”) is the angle that the line forms with the positive xxx-axis (you will meet the tangent tan⁡\tantan again in trigonometry).

  • m>0m > 0m>0: the line rises from left to right and forms an acute angle with the xxx-axis;
  • m<0m < 0m<0: the line falls, obtuse angle;
  • m=0m = 0m=0: horizontal line;
  • vertical line: mmm does not exist, because Δx=0\Delta x = 0Δx=0.

The larger ∣m∣|m|∣m∣, the steeper the line.

Example 5.5 Reading a line

y=−2x+3y = -2x + 3y=−2x+3 has m=−2m = -2m=−2 (it goes down by 222 for every step to the right) and q=3q = 3q=3, so it passes through (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3). It crosses the xxx-axis where y=0y = 0y=0: −2x+3=0-2x + 3 = 0−2x+3=0, that is x=32x = \frac{3}{2}x=23​. The point (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) belongs to the line, because −2⋅2+3=−1-2 \cdot 2 + 3 = -1−2⋅2+3=−1; the point (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) does not, because −2⋅1+3=1≠2-2 \cdot 1 + 3 = 1 \ne 2−2⋅1+3=1=2.

#General (implicit) form

Rule 5.3 All lines, and only lines

Every first-degree equation ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0, with aaa and bbb not both zero, represents a line; conversely, every line in the plane has an equation of this type, called the general (implicit) form. If b≠0b \ne 0b=0 you can solve for yyy: y=−abx−cby = -\frac{a}{b}x - \frac{c}{b}y=−ba​x−bc​, so

m=−ab,q=−cbm = -\frac{a}{b}, \qquad q = -\frac{c}{b}m=−ba​,q=−bc​

Special cases:

  • b=0b = 0b=0: what remains is ax+c=0ax + c = 0ax+c=0, that is x=−cax = -\frac{c}{a}x=−ac​, a vertical line with no slope. It is the only case that the slope-intercept form does not cover.
  • a=0a = 0a=0: y=−cby = -\frac{c}{b}y=−bc​, a horizontal line.
  • c=0c = 0c=0: the line passes through the origin.

The same line has infinitely many general equations: multiplying all the coefficients by the same number k≠0k \ne 0k=0 does not change the line. For example 2x−y+1=02x - y + 1 = 02x−y+1=0 and 4x−2y+2=04x - 2y + 2 = 04x−2y+2=0 are the same line.

Example 5.6 From general to slope-intercept form

3x−2y+6=03x - 2y + 6 = 03x−2y+6=0. Isolate yyy: −2y=−3x−6-2y = -3x - 6−2y=−3x−6; divide by −2-2−2: y=32x+3y = \frac{3}{2}x + 3y=23​x+3. So m=32m = \frac{3}{2}m=23​ (with the formula: −ab=−3−2=32-\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{3}{-2} = \frac{3}{2}−ba​=−−23​=23​) and q=3q = 3q=3. Intersections with the axes: for x=0x = 0x=0 you find y=3y = 3y=3, point (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3); for y=0y = 0y=0 you find 3x+6=03x + 6 = 03x+6=0, that is x=−2x = -2x=−2, point (−2,0)(-2, 0)(−2,0). Two points are enough to draw it.

Common mistake The sign of mmm

In ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0 the slope is −ab-\frac{a}{b}−ba​, with the minus sign in front. For 2x−4y+1=02x - 4y + 1 = 02x−4y+1=0: m=−2−4=12m = -\frac{2}{-4} = \frac{1}{2}m=−−42​=21​, not −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​. When in doubt, isolate yyy.

#Line through a point and line through two points

Rule 5.4 Line through a point with a given slope

The line that passes through P=(xP,yP)P = (x_P, y_P)P=(xP​,yP​) and has slope mmm is

y−yP=m(x−xP)y - y_P = m(x - x_P)y−yP​=m(x−xP​)

As mmm varies you get all the lines through PPP except the vertical one, x=xPx = x_Px=xP​.

Method Line through two points AAA and BBB
  1. If xA=xBx_A = x_BxA​=xB​ the line is vertical: x=xAx = x_Ax=xA​. If yA=yBy_A = y_ByA​=yB​ it is horizontal: y=yAy = y_Ay=yA​.
  2. Otherwise compute m=yB−yAxB−xAm = \frac{y_B - y_A}{x_B - x_A}m=xB​−xA​yB​−yA​​.
  3. Write y−yA=m(x−xA)y - y_A = m(x - x_A)y−yA​=m(x−xA​) and simplify.
  4. Check that BBB also satisfies the equation.

In one go you can use x−xAxB−xA=y−yAyB−yA\frac{x - x_A}{x_B - x_A} = \frac{y - y_A}{y_B - y_A}xB​−xA​x−xA​​=yB​−yA​y−yA​​, when the denominators are not zero.

Example 5.7 Two lines through two points

A=(1,2)A = (1, 2)A=(1,2), B=(3,8)B = (3, 8)B=(3,8): m=8−23−1=3m = \frac{8 - 2}{3 - 1} = 3m=3−18−2​=3; y−2=3(x−1)y - 2 = 3(x - 1)y−2=3(x−1), that is y=3x−1y = 3x - 1y=3x−1. Check with BBB: 3⋅3−1=83 \cdot 3 - 1 = 83⋅3−1=8.

A=(−2,5)A = (-2, 5)A=(−2,5), B=(4,2)B = (4, 2)B=(4,2): m=2−54−(−2)=−36=−12m = \frac{2 - 5}{4 - (-2)} = \frac{-3}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}m=4−(−2)2−5​=6−3​=−21​; y−5=−12(x+2)y - 5 = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 2)y−5=−21​(x+2), that is y=−12x+4y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 4y=−21​x+4, in general form x+2y−8=0x + 2y - 8 = 0x+2y−8=0. Check with BBB: −2+4=2-2 + 4 = 2−2+4=2.

#Intersection of two lines

A point common to two lines must satisfy both equations: you solve the system formed by the two equations, with the methods for linear systems. There are three cases:

  • exactly one solution: intersecting lines (different slopes);
  • no solution (impossible system): distinct parallel lines;
  • infinitely many solutions (indeterminate system): coincident lines.
Example 5.8 Where they meet

r:2x+y−7=0r: 2x + y - 7 = 0r:2x+y−7=0 and s:x−y−2=0s: x - y - 2 = 0s:x−y−2=0. Adding the two equations side by side: 3x−9=03x - 9 = 03x−9=0, so x=3x = 3x=3; from sss you get y=x−2=1y = x - 2 = 1y=x−2=1. The common point is (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1). Check in rrr: 6+1−7=06 + 1 - 7 = 06+1−7=0.

Example 5.9 Which plan is cheaper

To rent a bike, plan A costs €222 an hour; plan B costs a fixed €555 plus €111 an hour. With xxx = hours and yyy = cost in euros: A is the line y=2xy = 2xy=2x, B is the line y=x+5y = x + 5y=x+5. They meet where 2x=x+52x = x + 52x=x+5, that is for x=5x = 5x=5 (cost €101010). For less than 555 hours the line of A lies below that of B and A is cheaper; beyond 555 hours B is cheaper.

#Parallelism and perpendicularity

Rule 5.5 Parallel and perpendicular lines

For r:y=mx+qr: y = mx + qr:y=mx+q and r′:y=m′x+q′r': y = m'x + q'r′:y=m′x+q′:

  • rrr and r′r'r′ are parallel (r∥r′r \parallel r'r∥r′) if and only if m=m′m = m'm=m′;
  • rrr and r′r'r′ are perpendicular (r⊥r′r \perp r'r⊥r′) if and only if m⋅m′=−1m \cdot m' = -1m⋅m′=−1, that is m′=−1mm' = -\frac{1}{m}m′=−m1​: the slope of the perpendicular is the negative reciprocal (antireciproco).

In general form, ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0 and a′x+b′y+c′=0a'x + b'y + c' = 0a′x+b′y+c′=0 are parallel if ab′=a′bab' = a'bab′=a′b and perpendicular if aa′+bb′=0aa' + bb' = 0aa′+bb′=0. These two conditions also hold for horizontal and vertical lines: two vertical lines are parallel, a horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.

Example 5.10 Parallel and perpendicular through a point

Line through P=(2,−1)P = (2, -1)P=(2,−1) parallel to r:y=3x+5r: y = 3x + 5r:y=3x+5: same slope 333, so y+1=3(x−2)y + 1 = 3(x - 2)y+1=3(x−2), that is y=3x−7y = 3x - 7y=3x−7. Line through PPP perpendicular to rrr: slope −13-\frac{1}{3}−31​, so y+1=−13(x−2)y + 1 = -\frac{1}{3}(x - 2)y+1=−31​(x−2), that is y=−13x−13y = -\frac{1}{3}x - \frac{1}{3}y=−31​x−31​.

With the general form: 2x−3y+1=02x - 3y + 1 = 02x−3y+1=0 and 6x−9y+4=06x - 9y + 4 = 06x−9y+4=0 are parallel, because 2⋅(−9)=6⋅(−3)=−182 \cdot (-9) = 6 \cdot (-3) = -182⋅(−9)=6⋅(−3)=−18; 2x−3y+1=02x - 3y + 1 = 02x−3y+1=0 and 3x+2y−5=03x + 2y - 5 = 03x+2y−5=0 are perpendicular, because 2⋅3+(−3)⋅2=02 \cdot 3 + (-3) \cdot 2 = 02⋅3+(−3)⋅2=0.

Common mistake Negative reciprocal, not just the opposite

The perpendicular to a line with slope 23\frac{2}{3}32​ has slope −32-\frac{3}{2}−23​: you change the sign and turn the fraction upside down. Writing −23-\frac{2}{3}−32​ (only the opposite) or 32\frac{3}{2}23​ (only the reciprocal) are typical mistakes.

#Distance from a point to a line

Rule 5.6 Point-to-line distance

The distance of P0=(x0,y0)P_0 = (x_0, y_0)P0​=(x0​,y0​) from the line r:ax+by+c=0r: ax + by + c = 0r:ax+by+c=0 is

d(P0,r)=∣ax0+by0+c∣a2+b2d(P_0, r) = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}d(P0​,r)=a2+b2​∣ax0​+by0​+c∣​

It is the length of the segment P0HP_0HP0​H, where HHH is the foot of the perpendicular drawn from P0P_0P0​ to rrr. If P0P_0P0​ lies on the line, the numerator is 000.

The line must be written in general form. For lines parallel to the axes it is simpler: the distance of P0P_0P0​ from the line x=hx = hx=h is ∣x0−h∣|x_0 - h|∣x0​−h∣, from the line y=ky = ky=k it is ∣y0−k∣|y_0 - k|∣y0​−k∣.

Example 5.11 Two distances

P=(2,−1)P = (2, -1)P=(2,−1) and r:3x+4y+8=0r: 3x + 4y + 8 = 0r:3x+4y+8=0: d=∣3⋅2+4⋅(−1)+8∣9+16=∣10∣5=2d = \frac{|3 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot (-1) + 8|}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \frac{|10|}{5} = 2d=9+16​∣3⋅2+4⋅(−1)+8∣​=5∣10∣​=2. If the line is given in slope-intercept form, for example y=2x−3y = 2x - 3y=2x−3, first bring it to the form 2x−y−3=02x - y - 3 = 02x−y−3=0. The distance of the origin from it is then ∣−3∣4+1=35=355\frac{|-3|}{\sqrt{4 + 1}} = \frac{3}{\sqrt5} = \frac{3\sqrt5}{5}4+1​∣−3∣​=5​3​=535​​.

#Pencils of lines

Definition 5.3 Pencils of lines

The improper pencil (fascio improprio) is the set of all the lines parallel to a given line: y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q with mmm fixed and qqq varying; the vertical lines form the pencil x=kx = kx=k, with kkk varying. The proper pencil (fascio proprio) with centre C=(xC,yC)C = (x_C, y_C)C=(xC​,yC​) is the set of all the lines through CCC: y−yC=m(x−xC)y - y_C = m(x - x_C)y−yC​=m(x−xC​) as mmm varies, plus the vertical line x=xCx = x_Cx=xC​. If two lines ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0 and a′x+b′y+c′=0a'x + b'y + c' = 0a′x+b′y+c′=0 meet at CCC, the proper pencil can also be written λ(ax+by+c)+μ(a′x+b′y+c′)=0\lambda(ax + by + c) + \mu(a'x + b'y + c') = 0λ(ax+by+c)+μ(a′x+b′y+c′)=0, with λ\lambdaλ (lambda) and μ\muμ (mu) real numbers that are not both zero.

Example 5.12 Choosing a line of the pencil

The pencil y−2=m(x−1)y - 2 = m(x - 1)y−2=m(x−1) has centre (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2). Which of its lines also passes through (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6)? Substitute: 6−2=m(3−1)6 - 2 = m(3 - 1)6−2=m(3−1), so m=2m = 2m=2, and the line is y−2=2(x−1)y - 2 = 2(x - 1)y−2=2(x−1), that is y=2xy = 2xy=2x.

Method Centre of a pencil written with a parameter

An equation such as (k+1)x−y+2k=0(k + 1)x - y + 2k = 0(k+1)x−y+2k=0, with kkk a parameter, represents a different line for each value of kkk. Collect the terms in kkk: k(x+2)+(x−y)=0k(x + 2) + (x - y) = 0k(x+2)+(x−y)=0. The centre makes both brackets zero, whatever kkk is: x+2=0x + 2 = 0x+2=0 and x−y=0x - y = 0x−y=0, so C=(−2,−2)C = (-2, -2)C=(−2,−2). Watch out: with a single parameter, the very line that multiplies kkk is missing (here the vertical line x=−2x = -2x=−2), which no value of kkk produces. That is why the general form uses two parameters, λ\lambdaλ and μ\muμ.

In the test Lines in the test questions

In the questions with a choice of four answers it pays to check the options instead of redoing everything: substitute the given point (discard the lines that do not pass through it), then compare the slopes. For a line in general form use m=−abm = -\frac{a}{b}m=−ba​ straight away. With a parameter kkk (“for which kkk is the line parallel, perpendicular, through…”) write mmm as a function of kkk and impose the condition: the result is a number, suitable for a numeric answer.

#5.2 Conic sections

Circle, parabola, ellipse and hyperbola are called conics (conic sections). They are all described by second-degree equations in xxx and yyy.

Note Why “conics”

They are the curves you get by cutting a right circular cone with a plane (imagine two infinite ice-cream cones joined at the tip). A plane perpendicular to the axis of the cone gives a circle; a slightly tilted plane gives an ellipse; a plane parallel to a line of the cone gives a parabola; a plane that cuts both parts of the cone gives a hyperbola. If the plane passes through the vertex you get the degenerate conics: the vertex alone, or two intersecting lines, or two coincident lines.

#The circle

Definition 5.4 Circle

The circle (circonferenza) with centre CCC and radius r>0r > 0r>0 is the locus of the points PPP of the plane at distance rrr from CCC: d(P,C)=rd(P, C) = rd(P,C)=r. “Locus” means: the set of all and only the points with that property.

With C=(α,β)C = (\alpha, \beta)C=(α,β) (read “alpha” and “beta”), the distance formula, squared, gives the equation.

Rule 5.7 Equation of the circle
(x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2(x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2 = r^2(x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2

Expanding the squares you get the form x2+y2+ax+by+c=0x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0x2+y2+ax+by+c=0, from which

C=(−a2,−b2),r=a24+b24−cC = \left(-\frac{a}{2}, -\frac{b}{2}\right), \qquad r = \sqrt{\frac{a^2}{4} + \frac{b^2}{4} - c}C=(−2a​,−2b​),r=4a2​+4b2​−c​

The equation represents a real circle only if a24+b24−c≥0\frac{a^2}{4} + \frac{b^2}{4} - c \ge 04a2​+4b2​−c≥0, that is a2+b2−4c≥0a^2 + b^2 - 4c \ge 0a2+b2−4c≥0; if this quantity is 000, the “circle” reduces to the centre alone.

You recognise it like this: a second-degree equation in xxx and yyy, without the xyxyxy term, with equal coefficients of x2x^2x2 and y2y^2y2. If they are not 111, first divide the whole equation by that number.

Example 5.13 From centre and radius to the equation, and back

Centre (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) and radius 333: (x−2)2+(y+1)2=9(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 9(x−2)2+(y+1)2=9, that is x2−4x+4+y2+2y+1−9=0x^2 - 4x + 4 + y^2 + 2y + 1 - 9 = 0x2−4x+4+y2+2y+1−9=0, or x2+y2−4x+2y−4=0x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y - 4 = 0x2+y2−4x+2y−4=0.

Back: in x2+y2−4x+2y−4=0x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 2y - 4 = 0x2+y2−4x+2y−4=0 you have a=−4a = -4a=−4, b=2b = 2b=2, c=−4c = -4c=−4. Centre (−−42,−22)=(2,−1)\left(-\frac{-4}{2}, -\frac{2}{2}\right) = (2, -1)(−2−4​,−22​)=(2,−1), radius 4+1+4=3\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 34+1+4​=3.

The equation 2x2+2y2−8x+4y−8=02x^2 + 2y^2 - 8x + 4y - 8 = 02x2+2y2−8x+4y−8=0, divided by 222, is the same circle.

Example 5.14 A circle through the origin and a non-real circle

x2+y2−6x+8y=0x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 8y = 0x2+y2−6x+8y=0: centre (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4), radius 9+16−0=5\sqrt{9 + 16 - 0} = 59+16−0​=5. The constant term is 000, so it passes through the origin. x2+y2+2x−4y+10=0x^2 + y^2 + 2x - 4y + 10 = 0x2+y2+2x−4y+10=0: the “centre” would be (−1,2)(-1, 2)(−1,2), but 1+4−10=−5<01 + 4 - 10 = -5 < 01+4−10=−5<0. No real point satisfies the equation: it is not a circle.

Method Circle through three points

Three non-collinear points determine exactly one circle. Substitute their coordinates into x2+y2+ax+by+c=0x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0x2+y2+ax+by+c=0: you get a linear system of three equations in the unknowns aaa, bbb, ccc. With O=(0,0)O = (0, 0)O=(0,0), A=(4,0)A = (4, 0)A=(4,0), B=(0,2)B = (0, 2)B=(0,2): from OOO you get c=0c = 0c=0; from AAA: 16+4a=016 + 4a = 016+4a=0, a=−4a = -4a=−4; from BBB: 4+2b=04 + 2b = 04+2b=0, b=−2b = -2b=−2. The circle is x2+y2−4x−2y=0x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 2y = 0x2+y2−4x−2y=0, with centre (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1) and radius 4+1=5\sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt54+1​=5​. Alternatively, the centre is the point where the perpendicular bisectors of two chords meet (the perpendicular bisector of a segment is the line perpendicular to the segment through its midpoint), for example those of the segments OAOAOA and OBOBOB: x=2x = 2x=2 and y=1y = 1y=1.

Common mistake Centre with the signs changed

The centre has coordinates −a2-\frac{a}{2}−2a​ and −b2-\frac{b}{2}−2b​: for x2+y2+6x−2y=0x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 2y = 0x2+y2+6x−2y=0 the centre is (−3,1)(-3, 1)(−3,1), not (3,−1)(3, -1)(3,−1). And in the form (x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2(x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2 = r^2(x−α)2+(y−β)2=r2 the right-hand side is r2r^2r2: if you find 252525, the radius is 555.

#Line and circle

Rule 5.8 Position of a line relative to a circle

Let ddd be the distance of the centre CCC from the line and rrr the radius:

  • d>rd > rd>r: non-intersecting line (retta esterna), no common point;
  • d=rd = rd=r: tangent line, exactly one common point;
  • d<rd < rd<r: secant line, two common points.

You get the same result by putting the line and the circle into a system: the second-degree equation you obtain has Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0, Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 or Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0.

Example 5.15 Three lines and the circle x2+y2=25x^2 + y^2 = 25x2+y2=25

Centre OOO, radius 555.

  • 3x+4y−25=03x + 4y - 25 = 03x+4y−25=0: d=∣−25∣5=5=rd = \frac{|-25|}{5} = 5 = rd=5∣−25∣​=5=r, tangent. The point of contact is T=(3,4)T = (3, 4)T=(3,4): it lies on both, because 9+16=259 + 16 = 259+16=25 and 9+16−25=09 + 16 - 25 = 09+16−25=0.
  • y=x−1y = x - 1y=x−1: substituting, x2+(x−1)2=25x^2 + (x - 1)^2 = 25x2+(x−1)2=25, that is 2x2−2x−24=02x^2 - 2x - 24 = 02x2−2x−24=0, or x2−x−12=0x^2 - x - 12 = 0x2−x−12=0, with solutions x=4x = 4x=4 and x=−3x = -3x=−3. Secant at the points (4,3)(4, 3)(4,3) and (−3,−4)(-3, -4)(−3,−4).
  • y=x+8y = x + 8y=x+8, that is x−y+8=0x - y + 8 = 0x−y+8=0: d=82=42d = \frac{8}{\sqrt2} = 4\sqrt2d=2​8​=42​, about 5.66>55.66 > 55.66>5. Non-intersecting.
Method Tangent at a point of the circle

The tangent at a point P0P_0P0​ of the circle is perpendicular to the radius CP0CP_0CP0​. So compute the slope of CP0CP_0CP0​, take the negative reciprocal and write the line through P0P_0P0​. For x2+y2=25x^2 + y^2 = 25x2+y2=25 at T=(3,4)T = (3, 4)T=(3,4): the line OTOTOT has slope 43\frac{4}{3}34​, the tangent has slope −34-\frac{3}{4}−43​: y−4=−34(x−3)y - 4 = -\frac{3}{4}(x - 3)y−4=−43​(x−3), that is 3x+4y−25=03x + 4y - 25 = 03x+4y−25=0, the line of the previous example. If CP0CP_0CP0​ is horizontal the tangent is vertical, and vice versa.

#Pencils of circles

Given two circles with different centres, C1:x2+y2+a1x+b1y+c1=0C_1: x^2 + y^2 + a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0C1​:x2+y2+a1​x+b1​y+c1​=0 and C2:x2+y2+a2x+b2y+c2=0C_2: x^2 + y^2 + a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0C2​:x2+y2+a2​x+b2​y+c2​=0, the pencil they determine is

λ(x2+y2+a1x+b1y+c1)+μ(x2+y2+a2x+b2y+c2)=0\lambda(x^2 + y^2 + a_1x + b_1y + c_1) + \mu(x^2 + y^2 + a_2x + b_2y + c_2) = 0λ(x2+y2+a1​x+b1​y+c1​)+μ(x2+y2+a2​x+b2​y+c2​)=0
  • if λ+μ≠0\lambda + \mu \ne 0λ+μ=0 you get a circle (divide by λ+μ\lambda + \muλ+μ);
  • if λ+μ=0\lambda + \mu = 0λ+μ=0 the second-degree terms disappear and a line remains, the radical axis. In practice you find it by subtracting the two equations: (a1−a2)x+(b1−b2)y+(c1−c2)=0(a_1 - a_2)x + (b_1 - b_2)y + (c_1 - c_2) = 0(a1​−a2​)x+(b1​−b2​)y+(c1​−c2​)=0.
Rule 5.9 Properties of the pencil of circles
  • The points common to C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ belong to all the circles of the pencil and to the radical axis.
  • The centres of all the circles of the pencil lie on the line of centres (asse centrale), the line through the centres of C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​; the radical axis is perpendicular to the line of centres.
  • If C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ cut each other at two points, the radical axis is the line through those points; if they are tangent, it passes through the point of contact; if they have no common points, the radical axis does not meet any circle of the pencil.
  • Through every point of the plane passes one element of the pencil (a circle or the radical axis): the pencil “fills” the plane.
Example 5.16 Two circles that cut each other

C1:x2+y2−4=0C_1: x^2 + y^2 - 4 = 0C1​:x2+y2−4=0 (centre OOO, radius 222) and C2:x2+y2−4x=0C_2: x^2 + y^2 - 4x = 0C2​:x2+y2−4x=0 (centre (2,0)(2, 0)(2,0), radius 222). Radical axis: (x2+y2−4)−(x2+y2−4x)=4x−4=0(x^2 + y^2 - 4) - (x^2 + y^2 - 4x) = 4x - 4 = 0(x2+y2−4)−(x2+y2−4x)=4x−4=0, that is x=1x = 1x=1. Common points: with x=1x = 1x=1 in C1C_1C1​ you find 1+y2=41 + y^2 = 41+y2=4, y=±3y = \pm\sqrt3y=±3​ (read “plus or minus”: y=3y = \sqrt3y=3​ or y=−3y = -\sqrt3y=−3​), so P1=(1,3)P_1 = (1, \sqrt3)P1​=(1,3​) and P2=(1,−3)P_2 = (1, -\sqrt3)P2​=(1,−3​). The line of centres is the xxx-axis, perpendicular to x=1x = 1x=1. Circle of the pencil through (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0): substituting into λ(x2+y2−4)+μ(x2+y2−4x)=0\lambda(x^2 + y^2 - 4) + \mu(x^2 + y^2 - 4x) = 0λ(x2+y2−4)+μ(x2+y2−4x)=0 you find 5λ−3μ=05\lambda - 3\mu = 05λ−3μ=0. Choose λ=3\lambda = 3λ=3, μ=5\mu = 5μ=5: 8x2+8y2−20x−12=08x^2 + 8y^2 - 20x - 12 = 08x2+8y2−20x−12=0, that is x2+y2−52x−32=0x^2 + y^2 - \frac{5}{2}x - \frac{3}{2} = 0x2+y2−25​x−23​=0, with centre (54,0)\left(\frac{5}{4}, 0\right)(45​,0) on the line of centres and radius 74\frac{7}{4}47​.

#The parabola

Definition 5.5 Parabola

Given a point FFF, the focus, and a line fff that does not pass through FFF, the directrix, the parabola is the locus of the points PPP equidistant from the focus and from the directrix: d(P,F)=d(P,f)d(P, F) = d(P, f)d(P,F)=d(P,f). The point of the parabola closest to the focus and to the directrix is the vertex VVV; the line through FFF perpendicular to the directrix is the axis of symmetry.

Taking F=(0,c)F = (0, c)F=(0,c) and the directrix y=−cy = -cy=−c, the condition is x2+(y−c)2=∣y+c∣\sqrt{x^2 + (y - c)^2} = |y + c|x2+(y−c)2​=∣y+c∣; squaring and simplifying leaves x2=4cyx^2 = 4cyx2=4cy, that is y=14cx2y = \frac{1}{4c}x^2y=4c1​x2.

Rule 5.10 Parabola with its vertex at the origin
  • Focus (0,c)(0, c)(0,c) and directrix y=−cy = -cy=−c: the parabola is y=ax2y = ax^2y=ax2 with a=14ca = \frac{1}{4c}a=4c1​. Its axis is the yyy-axis; the focus is (0,14a)\left(0, \frac{1}{4a}\right)(0,4a1​) and the directrix y=−14ay = -\frac{1}{4a}y=−4a1​.
  • Focus (c,0)(c, 0)(c,0) and directrix x=−cx = -cx=−c: the parabola is x=ay2x = ay^2x=ay2, with the xxx-axis as its axis, focus (14a,0)\left(\frac{1}{4a}, 0\right)(4a1​,0) and directrix x=−14ax = -\frac{1}{4a}x=−4a1​.

In y=ax2y = ax^2y=ax2: if a>0a > 0a>0 the parabola is concave up (it opens upwards), if a<0a < 0a<0 it opens downwards; the larger ∣a∣|a|∣a∣, the narrower the parabola. In x=ay2x = ay^2x=ay2: it opens to the right if a>0a > 0a>0, to the left if a<0a < 0a<0.

Example 5.17 Focus and directrix

y=18x2y = \frac{1}{8}x^2y=81​x2: a=18a = \frac{1}{8}a=81​ and 14a=2\frac{1}{4a} = 24a1​=2, so focus (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2) and directrix y=−2y = -2y=−2. Check with the point (4,2)(4, 2)(4,2) of the parabola: it is at distance 444 from the focus and 2−(−2)=42 - (-2) = 42−(−2)=4 from the directrix. x=14y2x = \frac{1}{4}y^2x=41​y2: 14a=1\frac{1}{4a} = 14a1​=1, focus (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) and directrix x=−1x = -1x=−1.

Rule 5.11 Parabola with a vertical axis

y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c, with a≠0a \ne 0a=0 and Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac:

  • vertex V=(−b2a,−Δ4a)V = \left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{\Delta}{4a}\right)V=(−2ab​,−4aΔ​);
  • axis of symmetry x=−b2ax = -\frac{b}{2a}x=−2ab​;
  • focus F=(−b2a,1−Δ4a)F = \left(-\frac{b}{2a}, \frac{1 - \Delta}{4a}\right)F=(−2ab​,4a1−Δ​) and directrix y=−1+Δ4ay = -\frac{1 + \Delta}{4a}y=−4a1+Δ​;
  • it crosses the yyy-axis at (0,c)(0, c)(0,c) and the xxx-axis at the solutions of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0: two points if Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0, only one (the vertex) if Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, none if Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0.

aaa determines which way the parabola opens and how wide it is; bbb and ccc move the parabola.

For the yyy-coordinate of the vertex it is often easier to substitute xVx_VxV​ into the equation. The focus lies on the axis, at distance 14∣a∣\frac{1}{4|a|}4∣a∣1​ from the vertex, on the side towards which the parabola opens (“inside” the parabola); the directrix is perpendicular to the axis and lies at the same distance from the vertex, on the opposite side.

Example 5.18 All the elements of y=x2−4x+3y = x^2 - 4x + 3y=x2−4x+3

a=1a = 1a=1, b=−4b = -4b=−4, c=3c = 3c=3, Δ=16−12=4\Delta = 16 - 12 = 4Δ=16−12=4.

  • Vertex: xV=−−42=2x_V = -\frac{-4}{2} = 2xV​=−2−4​=2, yV=4−8+3=−1y_V = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1yV​=4−8+3=−1, so V=(2,−1)V = (2, -1)V=(2,−1) (with the formula: −44=−1-\frac{4}{4} = -1−44​=−1).
  • Axis x=2x = 2x=2; concave up.
  • Focus (2,1−44)=(2,−34)\left(2, \frac{1 - 4}{4}\right) = \left(2, -\frac{3}{4}\right)(2,41−4​)=(2,−43​); directrix y=−1+44=−54y = -\frac{1 + 4}{4} = -\frac{5}{4}y=−41+4​=−45​.
  • xxx-axis: x2−4x+3=0x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0x2−4x+3=0 for x=1x = 1x=1 and x=3x = 3x=3. yyy-axis: (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3).
Example 5.19 Concave down

y=−2x2+4xy = -2x^2 + 4xy=−2x2+4x: xV=−4−4=1x_V = -\frac{4}{-4} = 1xV​=−−44​=1, yV=−2+4=2y_V = -2 + 4 = 2yV​=−2+4=2, vertex (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2). Since a=−2<0a = -2 < 0a=−2<0 the focus lies below the vertex, at distance 18\frac{1}{8}81​: F=(1,158)F = \left(1, \frac{15}{8}\right)F=(1,815​); the directrix is y=178y = \frac{17}{8}y=817​. Zeros: −2x(x−2)=0-2x(x - 2) = 0−2x(x−2)=0, that is x=0x = 0x=0 and x=2x = 2x=2.

Method Finding a parabola from three conditions

To find aaa, bbb, ccc you need three conditions: passing through a point gives one, the vertex gives two.

  • Vertex (1,−3)(1, -3)(1,−3) and passing through (3,5)(3, 5)(3,5): use the form y=a(x−xV)2+yVy = a(x - x_V)^2 + y_Vy=a(x−xV​)2+yV​, here y=a(x−1)2−3y = a(x - 1)^2 - 3y=a(x−1)2−3. With (3,5)(3, 5)(3,5): 5=4a−35 = 4a - 35=4a−3, so a=2a = 2a=2 and y=2(x−1)2−3=2x2−4x−1y = 2(x - 1)^2 - 3 = 2x^2 - 4x - 1y=2(x−1)2−3=2x2−4x−1.
  • Passing through three points: substitute the three points into y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c and solve the linear system.
Note Parabola with a horizontal axis

x=ay2+by+cx = ay^2 + by + cx=ay2+by+c has the horizontal axis y=−b2ay = -\frac{b}{2a}y=−2ab​ and opens to the right if a>0a > 0a>0. For the vertex first compute yV=−b2ay_V = -\frac{b}{2a}yV​=−2ab​, then xVx_VxV​ by substituting. For example x=y2−2y−3x = y^2 - 2y - 3x=y2−2y−3 has yV=1y_V = 1yV​=1, xV=1−2−3=−4x_V = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4xV​=1−2−3=−4, vertex (−4,1)(-4, 1)(−4,1); it crosses the yyy-axis where y2−2y−3=0y^2 - 2y - 3 = 0y2−2y−3=0, that is at (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3) and (0,−1)(0, -1)(0,−1).

Line and parabola are studied like line and circle: you put them into a system and look at the Δ\DeltaΔ of the second-degree equation you get. For example y=x2y = x^2y=x2 and y=2x−1y = 2x - 1y=2x−1 give x2−2x+1=0x^2 - 2x + 1 = 0x2−2x+1=0, with Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0: the line is tangent at the point (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1). Watch out: a line parallel to the axis, such as x=1x = 1x=1, meets the parabola at only one point but is not tangent.

#Application: using the parabola to solve inequalities

Solving ax2+bx+c>0ax^2 + bx + c > 0ax2+bx+c>0 means finding the values of xxx where the parabola y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c lies above the xxx-axis; for <0< 0<0, those where it lies below. The solutions of the associated equation ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 are the xxx-coordinates of the points where the parabola meets the xxx-axis, that is the solutions of the system of y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c and y=0y = 0y=0.

Method Quadratic inequality using the parabola
  1. Bring everything to the left-hand side: ax2+bx+c>0ax^2 + bx + c > 0ax2+bx+c>0 (or <<<, ≥\ge≥, ≤\le≤).
  2. Solve the associated equation: you find the zeros x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​, only one if Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0, none if Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0.
  3. Sketch the parabola by hand: only the concavity (the sign of aaa) and the points on the xxx-axis matter.
  4. Read off the values of xxx where the graph lies above the axis (for >0> 0>0) or below it (for <0< 0<0); if there is an equals sign, include the zeros.

Summary for a>0a > 0a>0. If a<0a < 0a<0, first multiply both sides by −1-1−1, reversing the direction of the inequality (for example −x2+9>0-x^2 + 9 > 0−x2+9>0 becomes x2−9<0x^2 - 9 < 0x2−9<0), then use the table.

ax2+bx+c>0ax^2 + bx + c > 0ax2+bx+c>0x<x1x < x_1x<x1​ or x>x2x > x_2x>x2​every x≠x1x \ne x_1x=x1​every real xxx
ax2+bx+c<0ax^2 + bx + c < 0ax2+bx+c<0x1<x<x2x_1 < x < x_2x1​<x<x2​no xxxno xxx
ax2+bx+c≥0ax^2 + bx + c \ge 0ax2+bx+c≥0x≤x1x \le x_1x≤x1​ or x≥x2x \ge x_2x≥x2​every real xxxevery real xxx

Example 5.20 Four inequalities
  • x2−x−6<0x^2 - x - 6 < 0x2−x−6<0: zeros −2-2−2 and 333, parabola opening upwards, below the axis between the zeros: −2<x<3-2 < x < 3−2<x<3.
  • 2x2−3x≥02x^2 - 3x \ge 02x2−3x≥0: x(2x−3)=0x(2x - 3) = 0x(2x−3)=0 for x=0x = 0x=0 and x=32x = \frac{3}{2}x=23​; above the axis outside the zeros: x≤0x \le 0x≤0 or x≥32x \ge \frac{3}{2}x≥23​.
  • x2+2x+5>0x^2 + 2x + 5 > 0x2+2x+5>0: Δ=4−20<0\Delta = 4 - 20 < 0Δ=4−20<0, the parabola lies entirely above the axis: true for every real xxx.
  • −x2+4x−4≥0-x^2 + 4x - 4 \ge 0−x2+4x−4≥0: this is −(x−2)2≥0-(x - 2)^2 \ge 0−(x−2)2≥0. The parabola, opening downwards, touches the axis only at x=2x = 2x=2: the only solution is x=2x = 2x=2.
Common mistake “Or”, not “and”

For x2−x−6>0x^2 - x - 6 > 0x2−x−6>0 the solutions are x<−2x < -2x<−2 or x>3x > 3x>3: the union (−∞,−2)∪(3,+∞)(-\infty, -2) \cup (3, +\infty)(−∞,−2)∪(3,+∞). Writing “x<−2x < -2x<−2 and x>3x > 3x>3” means looking for a number that is less than −2-2−2 and at the same time greater than 333: there is none. Also pay attention to the endpoints: with <<< and >>> they are excluded (round bracket), with ≤\le≤ and ≥\ge≥ they are included (square bracket).

#The ellipse

Definition 5.6 Ellipse

Given two points FFF and F′F'F′, the foci, the ellipse is the locus of the points PPP for which the sum of the distances from the foci is constant: d(P,F)+d(P,F′)=2ad(P, F) + d(P, F') = 2ad(P,F)+d(P,F′)=2a, with 2a>d(F,F′)2a > d(F, F')2a>d(F,F′).

Rule 5.12 Standard equation of the ellipse

With the foci F=(c,0)F = (c, 0)F=(c,0) and F′=(−c,0)F' = (-c, 0)F′=(−c,0) on the xxx-axis and the centre at the origin:

x2a2+y2b2=1,b2=a2−c2(a>b)\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad b^2 = a^2 - c^2 \quad (a > b)a2x2​+b2y2​=1,b2=a2−c2(a>b)
  • vertices A=(a,0)A = (a, 0)A=(a,0), A′=(−a,0)A' = (-a, 0)A′=(−a,0), B=(0,b)B = (0, b)B=(0,b), B′=(0,−b)B' = (0, -b)B′=(0,−b); centre OOO;
  • symmetric with respect to both axes and to the origin; contained in the rectangle −a≤x≤a-a \le x \le a−a≤x≤a, −b≤y≤b-b \le y \le b−b≤y≤b;
  • eccentricity e=cae = \frac{c}{a}e=ac​, with 0≤e<10 \le e < 10≤e<1: the closer it is to 000, the “rounder” the ellipse. If a=ba = ba=b then c=0c = 0c=0 and the ellipse is a circle.

If in the equation b>ab > ab>a, the foci lie on the yyy-axis: (0,±c)(0, \pm c)(0,±c) with c2=b2−a2c^2 = b^2 - a^2c2=b2−a2, and the eccentricity is cb\frac{c}{b}bc​ (always the ratio between ccc and the semi-major axis).

In practice: the foci lie on the axis of the larger denominator and c2c^2c2 is the difference between the larger denominator and the smaller one. The relation a2=b2+c2a^2 = b^2 + c^2a2=b2+c2 can be seen at the vertex B=(0,b)B = (0, b)B=(0,b): it is at distance aaa from each focus (the sum is 2a2a2a), and aaa is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle with legs bbb and ccc.

Example 5.21 Reading an ellipse

x225+y29=1\frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 125x2​+9y2​=1: a=5a = 5a=5, b=3b = 3b=3 (roots of the denominators), c=25−9=4c = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4c=25−9​=4. Vertices (±5,0)(\pm 5, 0)(±5,0) and (0,±3)(0, \pm 3)(0,±3), foci (±4,0)(\pm 4, 0)(±4,0), eccentricity 45\frac{4}{5}54​. At the vertex B=(0,3)B = (0, 3)B=(0,3) the distances from the foci are 555 and 555, with sum 10=2a10 = 2a10=2a.

4x2+y2=164x^2 + y^2 = 164x2+y2=16: divide by 161616, x24+y216=1\frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{16} = 14x2​+16y2​=1. The larger denominator is under y2y^2y2: a=2a = 2a=2, b=4b = 4b=4, c=16−4=23c = \sqrt{16 - 4} = 2\sqrt3c=16−4​=23​. Vertices (±2,0)(\pm 2, 0)(±2,0) and (0,±4)(0, \pm 4)(0,±4), foci (0,±23)(0, \pm 2\sqrt3)(0,±23​) on the yyy-axis.

Common mistake First make the right-hand side equal to 1

Semi-axes and foci can be read off only when the right-hand side is 111: 9x2+4y2=369x^2 + 4y^2 = 369x2+4y2=36 must first be divided by 363636. And aaa is the root of the denominator: in x216\frac{x^2}{16}16x2​ the semi-axis is 444, not 161616.

#The hyperbola

Definition 5.7 Hyperbola

Given the foci FFF and F′F'F′, the hyperbola is the locus of the points PPP for which the difference of the distances from the foci, in absolute value, is constant: ∣d(P,F)−d(P,F′)∣=2a|d(P, F) - d(P, F')| = 2a∣d(P,F)−d(P,F′)∣=2a, with 2a<d(F,F′)2a < d(F, F')2a<d(F,F′).

Rule 5.13 Standard equation of the hyperbola

With the foci F=(c,0)F = (c, 0)F=(c,0) and F′=(−c,0)F' = (-c, 0)F′=(−c,0):

x2a2−y2b2=1,b2=c2−a2(c2=a2+b2)\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1, \qquad b^2 = c^2 - a^2 \quad (c^2 = a^2 + b^2)a2x2​−b2y2​=1,b2=c2−a2(c2=a2+b2)
  • vertices A=(a,0)A = (a, 0)A=(a,0) and A′=(−a,0)A' = (-a, 0)A′=(−a,0), where the hyperbola is tangent to the lines x=±ax = \pm ax=±a; no point on the yyy-axis and no point with −a<x<a-a < x < a−a<x<a, so the curve is made up of two branches;
  • symmetric with respect to both axes and to the origin;
  • asymptotes y=±baxy = \pm\frac{b}{a}xy=±ab​x: lines through the origin that the branches get closer and closer to without ever touching them; they are the diagonals of the rectangle with vertices (±a,±b)(\pm a, \pm b)(±a,±b);
  • eccentricity e=ca>1e = \frac{c}{a} > 1e=ac​>1.

The equation x2a2−y2b2=−1\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = -1a2x2​−b2y2​=−1 is a hyperbola with vertices (0,±b)(0, \pm b)(0,±b) and foci (0,±c)(0, \pm c)(0,±c) on the yyy-axis; the asymptotes are still y=±baxy = \pm\frac{b}{a}xy=±ab​x and again c2=a2+b2c^2 = a^2 + b^2c2=a2+b2.

A trick for the asymptotes: replace the right-hand side with 000. From x2a2−y2b2=0\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 0a2x2​−b2y2​=0 you get y2=b2a2x2y^2 = \frac{b^2}{a^2}x^2y2=a2b2​x2, that is y=±baxy = \pm\frac{b}{a}xy=±ab​x. The asymptotes split the lines through the origin into two families: for the hyperbola x2a2−y2b2=1\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1a2x2​−b2y2​=1, those with slope mmm such that ∣m∣<ba|m| < \frac{b}{a}∣m∣<ab​ cut it at two points, the others (asymptotes included) do not meet it.

x29−y216=1\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 19x2​−16y2​=1: a=3a = 3a=3, b=4b = 4b=4, c=9+16=5c = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5c=9+16​=5. Vertices (±3,0)(\pm 3, 0)(±3,0), foci (±5,0)(\pm 5, 0)(±5,0), asymptotes y=±43xy = \pm\frac{4}{3}xy=±34​x, eccentricity 53\frac{5}{3}35​.

4x2−9y2=−364x^2 - 9y^2 = -364x2−9y2=−36: divide by 363636, x29−y24=−1\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{4} = -19x2​−4y2​=−1. With the −1-1−1 the vertices lie on the yyy-axis: (0,±2)(0, \pm 2)(0,±2); c=9+4=13c = \sqrt{9 + 4} = \sqrt{13}c=9+4​=13​, foci (0,±13)(0, \pm\sqrt{13})(0,±13​); asymptotes y=±23xy = \pm\frac{2}{3}xy=±32​x.

#Rectangular hyperbola

Rule 5.14 Rectangular hyperbola

If a=ba = ba=b the hyperbola is called rectangular (iperbole equilatera): x2−y2=a2x^2 - y^2 = a^2x2−y2=a2. The asymptotes are the bisectors y=xy = xy=x and y=−xy = -xy=−x, perpendicular to each other; the foci are (±a2,0)(\pm a\sqrt2, 0)(±a2​,0) and the eccentricity is 2\sqrt22​. The equation x2−y2=0x^2 - y^2 = 0x2−y2=0, that is (x−y)(x+y)=0(x - y)(x + y) = 0(x−y)(x+y)=0, represents the two bisectors: it is a degenerate hyperbola.

Rule 5.15 Rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes

If the two asymptotes are taken as the Cartesian axes, the rectangular hyperbola has equation

xy=k(k≠0)xy = k \qquad (k \ne 0)xy=k(k=0)

The asymptotes are the xxx- and yyy-axes. If k>0k > 0k>0 the branches lie in quadrants I and III and the vertices are on the bisector y=xy = xy=x, at (k,k)(\sqrt{k}, \sqrt{k})(k​,k​) and (−k,−k)(-\sqrt{k}, -\sqrt{k})(−k​,−k​); the foci lie on the same bisector, at (2k,2k)(\sqrt{2k}, \sqrt{2k})(2k​,2k​) and (−2k,−2k)(-\sqrt{2k}, -\sqrt{2k})(−2k​,−2k​); if k<0k < 0k<0 the branches lie in quadrants II and IV and the vertices are on the bisector y=−xy = -xy=−x. It is the graph of y=kxy = \frac{k}{x}y=xk​, inverse proportionality.

Example 5.23 The hyperbola xy=4xy = 4xy=4

It passes through (1,4)(1, 4)(1,4), (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2), (4,1)(4, 1)(4,1) and through their symmetric points with respect to the origin, (−1,−4)(-1, -4)(−1,−4), (−2,−2)(-2, -2)(−2,−2), (−4,−1)(-4, -1)(−4,−1). The vertices are (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2) and (−2,−2)(-2, -2)(−2,−2): they are at distance 222\sqrt222​ from the origin, which is the semi-axis aaa (indeed k=a22=82=4k = \frac{a^2}{2} = \frac{8}{2} = 4k=2a2​=28​=4). The foci are (22,22)(2\sqrt2, 2\sqrt2)(22​,22​) and (−22,−22)(-2\sqrt2, -2\sqrt2)(−22​,−22​): they are at distance 4=a24 = a\sqrt24=a2​ from the origin, as in the rectangular hyperbola.

In the test Conics in the test questions

The most natural tasks are: recognise the conic from an equation, give the centre and radius of a circle, the vertex of a parabola, the foci or asymptotes of an ellipse or hyperbola, say whether a point lies on the curve, decide whether a line is tangent. For the point: substitute. For tangency: centre-to-line distance equal to the radius (circle) or Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 in the system (parabola). Before reading off aaa and bbb check that the right-hand side is 111, and remember: ellipse c2=a2−b2c^2 = a^2 - b^2c2=a2−b2 (subtract), hyperbola c2=a2+b2c^2 = a^2 + b^2c2=a2+b2 (add).

#Exercises

Exercise 5.1BasicDistance and midpoint

Given A=(−1,3)A = (-1, 3)A=(−1,3) and B=(5,−5)B = (5, -5)B=(5,−5), compute the distance ABABAB and the midpoint MMM. In which quadrant does MMM lie?

Solution

Differences: xB−xA=5−(−1)=6x_B - x_A = 5 - (-1) = 6xB​−xA​=5−(−1)=6 and yB−yA=−5−3=−8y_B - y_A = -5 - 3 = -8yB​−yA​=−5−3=−8.

d(A,B)=62+(−8)2=36+64=100=10d(A, B) = \sqrt{6^2 + (-8)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10d(A,B)=62+(−8)2​=36+64​=100​=10

Midpoint: M=(−1+52,3+(−5)2)=(2,−1)M = \left(\frac{-1 + 5}{2}, \frac{3 + (-5)}{2}\right) = (2, -1)M=(2−1+5​,23+(−5)​)=(2,−1). It has a positive xxx-coordinate and a negative yyy-coordinate: it lies in quadrant IV.

Exercise 5.2BasicLine through two points

Write the equation of the line through A=(2,−1)A = (2, -1)A=(2,−1) and B=(4,3)B = (4, 3)B=(4,3), in slope-intercept form and in general form. Find where it crosses the axes and decide whether P=(3,1)P = (3, 1)P=(3,1) and Q=(1,−2)Q = (1, -2)Q=(1,−2) belong to it.

Solution

m=3−(−1)4−2=42=2m = \frac{3 - (-1)}{4 - 2} = \frac{4}{2} = 2m=4−23−(−1)​=24​=2. Line through AAA: y+1=2(x−2)y + 1 = 2(x - 2)y+1=2(x−2), that is y=2x−5y = 2x - 5y=2x−5; in general form 2x−y−5=02x - y - 5 = 02x−y−5=0. Check with BBB: 2⋅4−5=32 \cdot 4 - 5 = 32⋅4−5=3.

yyy-axis (x=0x = 0x=0): y=−5y = -5y=−5, point (0,−5)(0, -5)(0,−5). xxx-axis (y=0y = 0y=0): 2x−5=02x - 5 = 02x−5=0, x=52x = \frac{5}{2}x=25​, point (52,0)\left(\frac{5}{2}, 0\right)(25​,0).

PPP: 2⋅3−5=12 \cdot 3 - 5 = 12⋅3−5=1, it belongs to the line. QQQ: 2⋅1−5=−3≠−22 \cdot 1 - 5 = -3 \ne -22⋅1−5=−3=−2, it does not belong to it.

Exercise 5.3BasicCentre and radius

Find the centre and radius of the circle x2+y2+6x−2y−6=0x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 2y - 6 = 0x2+y2+6x−2y−6=0. Does it pass through the origin?

Solution

a=6a = 6a=6, b=−2b = -2b=−2, c=−6c = -6c=−6. Centre (−62,−−22)=(−3,1)\left(-\frac{6}{2}, -\frac{-2}{2}\right) = (-3, 1)(−26​,−2−2​)=(−3,1). Radius r=9+1−(−6)=16=4r = \sqrt{9 + 1 - (-6)} = \sqrt{16} = 4r=9+1−(−6)​=16​=4.

It does not pass through the origin: substituting (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) leaves −6≠0-6 \ne 0−6=0. A circle passes through the origin only if the constant term is 000.

Exercise 5.4BasicThe elements of a parabola

For y=x2+2x−8y = x^2 + 2x - 8y=x2+2x−8 find the vertex, axis, focus, directrix and intersections with the axes.

Solution

a=1a = 1a=1, b=2b = 2b=2, c=−8c = -8c=−8, Δ=4+32=36\Delta = 4 + 32 = 36Δ=4+32=36.

Vertex: xV=−22=−1x_V = -\frac{2}{2} = -1xV​=−22​=−1, yV=1−2−8=−9y_V = 1 - 2 - 8 = -9yV​=1−2−8=−9, so V=(−1,−9)V = (-1, -9)V=(−1,−9). Axis x=−1x = -1x=−1. Concave up (a>0a > 0a>0).

Focus: (−1,1−364)=(−1,−354)\left(-1, \frac{1 - 36}{4}\right) = \left(-1, -\frac{35}{4}\right)(−1,41−36​)=(−1,−435​), that is 14\frac{1}{4}41​ above the vertex. Directrix: y=−1+364=−374y = -\frac{1 + 36}{4} = -\frac{37}{4}y=−41+36​=−437​, 14\frac{1}{4}41​ below the vertex.

xxx-axis: x2+2x−8=(x+4)(x−2)=0x^2 + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2) = 0x2+2x−8=(x+4)(x−2)=0, points (−4,0)(-4, 0)(−4,0) and (2,0)(2, 0)(2,0). yyy-axis: (0,−8)(0, -8)(0,−8).

Exercise 5.5BasicInequalities with the parabola

Solve: a) x2−5x+4≤0x^2 - 5x + 4 \le 0x2−5x+4≤0; b) −x2+9>0-x^2 + 9 > 0−x2+9>0; c) x2−6x+9>0x^2 - 6x + 9 > 0x2−6x+9>0; d) x2+x+1<0x^2 + x + 1 < 0x2+x+1<0.

Solution
  • a) Zeros 111 and 444; parabola opening upwards, below the axis (or on it) between the zeros: 1≤x≤41 \le x \le 41≤x≤4, that is [1,4][1, 4][1,4].
  • b) Zeros −3-3−3 and 333; a=−1<0a = -1 < 0a=−1<0, parabola opening downwards, above the axis between the zeros: −3<x<3-3 < x < 3−3<x<3.
  • c) x2−6x+9=(x−3)2x^2 - 6x + 9 = (x - 3)^2x2−6x+9=(x−3)2: the parabola touches the axis only at x=3x = 3x=3 and lies above it everywhere else. Solutions: every x≠3x \ne 3x=3.
  • d) Δ=1−4=−3<0\Delta = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0Δ=1−4=−3<0 and a>0a > 0a>0: the parabola lies entirely above the axis and is never negative. No solution.
Exercise 5.6IntermediateAn equidistant point

Find the point PPP on the yyy-axis that is at the same distance from A=(2,1)A = (2, 1)A=(2,1) and from B=(4,3)B = (4, 3)B=(4,3).

Solution

A point on the yyy-axis has the form P=(0,y)P = (0, y)P=(0,y). Impose d(P,A)2=d(P,B)2d(P, A)^2 = d(P, B)^2d(P,A)2=d(P,B)2, so that the roots disappear:

(0−2)2+(y−1)2=(0−4)2+(y−3)2(0 - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = (0 - 4)^2 + (y - 3)^2(0−2)2+(y−1)2=(0−4)2+(y−3)2

4+y2−2y+1=16+y2−6y+94 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = 16 + y^2 - 6y + 94+y2−2y+1=16+y2−6y+9. The y2y^2y2 terms cancel: −2y+5=−6y+25-2y + 5 = -6y + 25−2y+5=−6y+25, that is 4y=204y = 204y=20, y=5y = 5y=5.

P=(0,5)P = (0, 5)P=(0,5). Check: d(P,A)=4+16=20d(P, A) = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20}d(P,A)=4+16​=20​ and d(P,B)=16+4=20d(P, B) = \sqrt{16 + 4} = \sqrt{20}d(P,B)=16+4​=20​.

Exercise 5.7IntermediateParallel, perpendicular and distance

Given the line r:2x+3y−6=0r: 2x + 3y - 6 = 0r:2x+3y−6=0 and the point P=(−1,2)P = (-1, 2)P=(−1,2), write the line through PPP parallel to rrr and the line through PPP perpendicular to rrr; compute the distance of PPP from rrr.

Solution

mr=−23m_r = -\frac{2}{3}mr​=−32​.

Parallel: y−2=−23(x+1)y - 2 = -\frac{2}{3}(x + 1)y−2=−32​(x+1); multiplying by 333: 3y−6=−2x−23y - 6 = -2x - 23y−6=−2x−2, that is 2x+3y−4=02x + 3y - 4 = 02x+3y−4=0. It has the same aaa and bbb as rrr: only the constant term changes.

Perpendicular: slope 32\frac{3}{2}23​; y−2=32(x+1)y - 2 = \frac{3}{2}(x + 1)y−2=23​(x+1), that is 2y−4=3x+32y - 4 = 3x + 32y−4=3x+3, or 3x−2y+7=03x - 2y + 7 = 03x−2y+7=0. Check: 3⋅(−1)−2⋅2+7=03 \cdot (-1) - 2 \cdot 2 + 7 = 03⋅(−1)−2⋅2+7=0.

Distance: d=∣2⋅(−1)+3⋅2−6∣4+9=∣−2∣13=213=21313d = \frac{|2 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot 2 - 6|}{\sqrt{4 + 9}} = \frac{|-2|}{\sqrt{13}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} = \frac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}d=4+9​∣2⋅(−1)+3⋅2−6∣​=13​∣−2∣​=13​2​=13213​​.

Exercise 5.8IntermediateCircle tangent to a line

Write the equation of the circle with centre C=(2,3)C = (2, 3)C=(2,3) tangent to the line 3x+4y+2=03x + 4y + 2 = 03x+4y+2=0.

Solution

Tangent means that the radius equals the distance of the centre from the line:

r=∣3⋅2+4⋅3+2∣9+16=205=4r = \frac{|3 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 3 + 2|}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \frac{20}{5} = 4r=9+16​∣3⋅2+4⋅3+2∣​=520​=4

Equation: (x−2)2+(y−3)2=16(x - 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 16(x−2)2+(y−3)2=16, that is x2+y2−4x−6y+4+9−16=0x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 6y + 4 + 9 - 16 = 0x2+y2−4x−6y+4+9−16=0, or x2+y2−4x−6y−3=0x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 6y - 3 = 0x2+y2−4x−6y−3=0.

Exercise 5.9IntermediateCentre at the vertex of a parabola

Write the equation of the circle whose centre is the vertex of the parabola x=y2−2y−3x = y^2 - 2y - 3x=y2−2y−3 and which passes through the origin.

Solution

The parabola has a horizontal axis: yV=−−22=1y_V = -\frac{-2}{2} = 1yV​=−2−2​=1 and xV=1−2−3=−4x_V = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4xV​=1−2−3=−4, vertex (−4,1)(-4, 1)(−4,1).

The radius is the distance of the centre from the origin: r=16+1=17r = \sqrt{16 + 1} = \sqrt{17}r=16+1​=17​.

(x+4)2+(y−1)2=17(x + 4)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 17(x+4)2+(y−1)2=17, that is x2+y2+8x−2y+16+1−17=0x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 2y + 16 + 1 - 17 = 0x2+y2+8x−2y+16+1−17=0, or x2+y2+8x−2y=0x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 2y = 0x2+y2+8x−2y=0. The constant term is 000: the circle really does pass through the origin.

Exercise 5.10IntermediateEllipse and hyperbola

Find the vertices, foci and eccentricity of the ellipse 16x2+25y2=40016x^2 + 25y^2 = 40016x2+25y2=400; then the vertices, foci and asymptotes of the hyperbola 9x2−16y2=1449x^2 - 16y^2 = 1449x2−16y2=144.

Ellipse: divide by 400400400, x225+y216=1\frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{16} = 125x2​+16y2​=1. a=5a = 5a=5, b=4b = 4b=4, c=25−16=3c = \sqrt{25 - 16} = 3c=25−16​=3. Vertices (±5,0)(\pm 5, 0)(±5,0) and (0,±4)(0, \pm 4)(0,±4); foci (±3,0)(\pm 3, 0)(±3,0); eccentricity 35\frac{3}{5}53​.

Exercise 5.11Test levelA line with a parameter

Consider the lines (k−1)x+(k+1)y−4=0(k - 1)x + (k + 1)y - 4 = 0(k−1)x+(k+1)y−4=0, with kkk real. Find kkk so that the line: a) passes through (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3); b) is parallel to the xxx-axis; c) is parallel to the bisector of quadrants I and III; d) is perpendicular to y=13xy = \frac{1}{3}xy=31​x; e) is vertical; f) forms an acute angle with the xxx-axis. Finally, find the point through which all of them pass.

Solution

For k≠−1k \ne -1k=−1 the slope is m=−k−1k+1m = -\frac{k - 1}{k + 1}m=−k+1k−1​.

  • a) (k−1)⋅1+(k+1)⋅3−4=0(k - 1) \cdot 1 + (k + 1) \cdot 3 - 4 = 0(k−1)⋅1+(k+1)⋅3−4=0, that is 4k−2=04k - 2 = 04k−2=0, k=12k = \frac{1}{2}k=21​.
  • b) Horizontal: the coefficient of xxx must be zero, k=1k = 1k=1. Line 2y−4=02y - 4 = 02y−4=0, that is y=2y = 2y=2.
  • c) m=1m = 1m=1: −(k−1)=k+1-(k - 1) = k + 1−(k−1)=k+1, that is −k+1=k+1-k + 1 = k + 1−k+1=k+1, k=0k = 0k=0. Line −x+y−4=0-x + y - 4 = 0−x+y−4=0, that is y=x+4y = x + 4y=x+4.
  • d) m=−3m = -3m=−3: −(k−1)=−3(k+1)-(k - 1) = -3(k + 1)−(k−1)=−3(k+1), that is −k+1=−3k−3-k + 1 = -3k - 3−k+1=−3k−3, 2k=−42k = -42k=−4, k=−2k = -2k=−2.
  • e) Vertical: the coefficient of yyy must be zero, k=−1k = -1k=−1. Line −2x−4=0-2x - 4 = 0−2x−4=0, that is x=−2x = -2x=−2.
  • f) An acute angle means m>0m > 0m>0: −k−1k+1>0-\frac{k - 1}{k + 1} > 0−k+1k−1​>0, that is k−1k+1<0\frac{k - 1}{k + 1} < 0k+1k−1​<0. Numerator and denominator must have opposite signs: −1<k<1-1 < k < 1−1<k<1.

Common point: collect the terms in kkk, k(x+y)+(−x+y−4)=0k(x + y) + (-x + y - 4) = 0k(x+y)+(−x+y−4)=0. You need x+y=0x + y = 0x+y=0 and −x+y−4=0-x + y - 4 = 0−x+y−4=0; adding them, 2y−4=02y - 4 = 02y−4=0, so y=2y = 2y=2 and x=−2x = -2x=−2. All the lines pass through (−2,2)(-2, 2)(−2,2): indeed the lines found in b) and e) are y=2y = 2y=2 and x=−2x = -2x=−2.

y−6=34(x+2)y - 6 = \frac{3}{4}(x + 2)y−6=43​(x+2); multiplying by 444: 4y−24=3x+64y - 24 = 3x + 64y−24=3x+6, that is 3x−4y+30=03x - 4y + 30 = 03x−4y+30=0.

For which values of qqq is the line y=x+qy = x + qy=x+q tangent to the circle x2+y2=8x^2 + y^2 = 8x2+y2=8? For which values is it secant?

Solution

Exercise 5.14Test levelParabola through three points

Find the parabola y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c that passes through (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1), (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) and (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3), and its vertex.

Solution

From (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1): c=1c = 1c=1. From (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0): a+b+1=0a + b + 1 = 0a+b+1=0, that is a+b=−1a + b = -1a+b=−1. From (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3): 4a+2b+1=34a + 2b + 1 = 34a+2b+1=3, that is 2a+b=12a + b = 12a+b=1.

Subtracting the second from the third: a=2a = 2a=2, so b=−3b = -3b=−3. The parabola is y=2x2−3x+1y = 2x^2 - 3x + 1y=2x2−3x+1.

Vertex: xV=34x_V = \frac{3}{4}xV​=43​, yV=2⋅916−94+1=98−188+88=−18y_V = 2 \cdot \frac{9}{16} - \frac{9}{4} + 1 = \frac{9}{8} - \frac{18}{8} + \frac{8}{8} = -\frac{1}{8}yV​=2⋅169​−49​+1=89​−818​+88​=−81​. So V=(34,−18)V = \left(\frac{3}{4}, -\frac{1}{8}\right)V=(43​,−81​).

Exercise 5.15Test levelParabola above a line

For which xxx does the parabola y=x2−2x−3y = x^2 - 2x - 3y=x2−2x−3 lie above the line y=x+1y = x + 1y=x+1? At which points do they meet?

Solution

“Above” means x2−2x−3>x+1x^2 - 2x - 3 > x + 1x2−2x−3>x+1, that is x2−3x−4>0x^2 - 3x - 4 > 0x2−3x−4>0. Zeros: (x−4)(x+1)=0(x - 4)(x + 1) = 0(x−4)(x+1)=0, x=−1x = -1x=−1 and x=4x = 4x=4. The associated parabola opens upwards: it is positive outside the zeros, so x<−1x < -1x<−1 or x>4x > 4x>4.

Meeting points: for x=−1x = -1x=−1 you have y=0y = 0y=0, for x=4x = 4x=4 you have y=5y = 5y=5: (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (4,5)(4, 5)(4,5).

  15. For which value of kkk is the line (k−1)x+2y−3=0(k - 1)x + 2y - 3 = 0(k−1)x+2y−3=0 perpendicular to the line y=12xy = \frac{1}{2}xy=21​x?
    5
    The slope m=−k−12m = -\frac{k - 1}{2}m=−2k−1​ must be the negative reciprocal of 12\frac{1}{2}21​, that is −2-2−2: k−12=2\frac{k - 1}{2} = 22k−1​=2, so k=5k = 5k=5.
  16. In which quadrants does the hyperbola xy=−6xy = -6xy=−6 lie?
    xy=−6<0xy = -6 < 0xy=−6<0 means that xxx and yyy have opposite signs: quadrant II (x<0x < 0x<0, y>0y > 0y>0) and quadrant IV (x>0x > 0x>0, y<0y < 0y<0).

Known errata in this material

In the material of this module we found a few errata, checked against the original pages and PDFs; the notes give the correct version.

  • Libro 5.2, circle, tangent line to x2+y2+6x−4y=0x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 4y = 0x2+y2+6x−4y=0 at the point P0=(−6,4)P_0 = (-6, 4)P0​=(−6,4): the line through P0P_0P0​ with slope 32\frac{3}{2}23​ is written y−4=32(x+6)y - 4 = \frac{3}{2}(x + 6)y−4=23​(x+6). The book writes y−2=32(x+3)y - 2 = \frac{3}{2}(x + 3)y−2=23​(x+3), which passes through the centre (−3,2)(-3, 2)(−3,2); the final result, y=32x+13y = \frac{3}{2}x + 13y=23​x+13, is correct.
